Page 27 of 54 DE-EE0009512 Massachusetts Institute of Technology Project 5: 2D/3D interface reconstruction for perovskite solar cells In the conventional 2D/3D perovskite passivation method, previously published works encountered challenges such as an impure 2D perovskite phase, a wide bandgap type I band alignment and a residual PbI . To solve these challenges, we propose and test a new 2D/3D 2 interface reconstruction method to grow the 2D perovskite. The procedure and the in-situ GIWAX result of the method are shown in Figures 5.1.a and 1.b, respectively. First, instead of loading the optimized amount of the 2D ligand on top of the 3D perovskite, we overload the 2D ligand amount. The excess of the 2D ligand forces most of the residual PbI to react with the 2D ligand and form 2 the 2D perovskite. As shown in Figure 5.1.b, most of the PbI disappears after overloading, and 2 two 2D perovskite phases (n=1 and n=2) form after heating. Second, to remove the excess 2D ligand and control the 2D perovskite thickness, we use isopropanol (IPA) to wash the 2D perovskite surface. As shown in Figure 5.1.b, we are effective in washing away n=1 2D perovskite and keeping just the right amount of n=2 2D perovskite on the surface. Finally, we anneal the film to form a more crystalline 2D perovskite structure. Figure 5.1. a. The procedure of the 2D/3D interface reconstruction method. b. The corresponding in-situ GIWAX data for the 2D/3D interface reconstruction method. To further understand the mechanism of the interface reconstruction, we compared the static XRD spectrum of several methods for forming the perovskite films: the conventional 2D deposit method (2D control), 2D control washed with IPA, and the interface reconstruction method, as illustrated in Figures 5.2a and 5.2b. After washing the 2D control film with IPA, the Page 28 of 54 DE-EE0009512 Massachusetts Institute of Technology 2D perovskite on the film is washed away, and there is additional residual PbI , as shown in Figure 2 5.2a. This is because the 2D perovskite film in the 2D control sample is one thin layer, and IPA can dissolve both the 2D perovskite and the organic molecules.
